/blog/make-social-media-automation.html:
Make.com social media automation: one scenario, every network

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-11-26 · 7 min read

Make has modules for a few networks, but each needs its own connection and some have been withdrawn. One HTTP module that calls a posting API covers all of them. Here is the scenario, with the exact module settings.

Short answer: let Make do what it is good at (watching a Google Sheet, an RSS feed or a form, and shaping the text with an AI module), then send the finished post to one publishing API with Make's HTTP → Make a request module. The API posts to every account you connected, so you don't need one module and one connection per network.

The HTTP module is a built-in Make app and works on the free plan. Each run uses operations from your monthly allowance, so check your plan's limit against how often the scenario runs.

Why not use Make's social media modules?

Make has apps for some networks, such as Facebook Pages and LinkedIn. But coverage changes when networks change their APIs (Make's own community has threads on posting to X by HTTP after its X app was withdrawn), TikTok, Threads and Bluesky usually mean raw API calls anyway, and each network is another connection to keep authorized. One posting API keeps the scenario to a single module.

Step 1: API key and account IDs

  1. In Social0, connect your networks under Connections, then create an API key under Developer → API keys (sk_live_…, shown once).
  2. In Make, add an HTTP → Make a request module: URL https://api.social0.app/v1/accounts, method GET, and a header Authorization = Bearer sk_live_….
  3. Click Run once and copy the id of each account you want to post to. Then delete this module or keep it disabled.

Step 2: the posting module

Module:        HTTP → Make a request
URL:           https://api.social0.app/v1/posts/schedule
Method:        POST
Headers:       Authorization = Bearer sk_live_…
Body type:     Raw
Content type:  JSON (application/json)
Request content:
{
  "content": "{{1.text}}",
  "platforms": ["ACCOUNT_ID_1", "ACCOUNT_ID_2"],
  "scheduledAt": "{{1.publish_at}}"
}
Parse response: Yes
  • Replace 1.text and 1.publish_at with the fields from your trigger module.
  • Post now instead: change the URL to /v1/posts/publish and remove scheduledAt.
  • Time format: an ISO time such as 2026-12-01T09:00:00Z, an offset like +05:30, or your local time followed by +default (e.g. 2026-12-01T09:00:00+default) to use the time zone in your Social0 settings; up to a year ahead.
  • Quotes and line breaks in the text can break raw JSON. Wrap the field with Make's replace() function, or build the body with a JSON → Create JSON module first.

Step 3: a trigger

  • Google Sheets calendar: Google Sheets → Watch New Rows (or Search Rows where Status is "ready") → posting module → Update a Row to mark it scheduled, so the next run skips it. The content calendar guide has a column layout.
  • Blog to social: RSS → Watch RSS feed items → an AI module that writes a short post from the title and summary → posting module.
  • Form or Airtable: watch new records from a submission form or base, then post. Good for teams where several people suggest posts.
Add a review step for AI posts If an AI module writes the text, send it to Slack or email first and only post after someone approves it. A scenario that posts unreviewed AI text to nine networks can embarrass you nine times at once.

Step 4: catch failures

Publishing happens after the API replies (it returns 202 with status: "queued"), so a successful HTTP module doesn't mean the post is live. Create a second scenario that starts with Webhooks → Custom webhook, register its URL in Social0 for post.failed (and post.published if you want a log), and send failures to Slack or email. Why scheduled posts fail explains the usual causes.

Images and video

Attaching media takes three HTTP modules: POST /v1/media/presign to get an upload URL, an HTTP PUT of the file to that URL, then POST /v1/media/confirm to get a media ID you add to the post's media array. Check the file against each network's specs first: image sizes and video specs.

Post to 9 networks from one Make module. The API is on every plan, including Free. See the Social0 API

Using n8n instead? The same setup is in the n8n guide, and the Zapier guide covers Zapier.

Frequently asked questions

Can Make.com post to social media automatically?

Yes. Use a trigger such as Google Sheets, RSS or a form, then either a network's own Make app or one HTTP module that calls a posting API like Social0's to publish to several networks at once.

Does the HTTP module work on Make's free plan?

Yes. HTTP is a built-in Make app. Every run uses operations from your plan's monthly allowance, so match how often the scenario runs to your limit.

Can Make post to TikTok, Threads and Bluesky?

Through a posting API, yes: the same HTTP request that posts to X or LinkedIn posts to TikTok, Threads and Bluesky if those accounts are connected in Social0.

How do I schedule posts from Make?

Send the post to an endpoint that accepts a future time, such as Social0's /v1/posts/schedule with a scheduledAt field. The scenario finishes straight away and the post goes out at that time.

Why does my Make HTTP request fail with a JSON error?

Usually quotes or line breaks in the post text break the raw JSON. Build the body with a JSON → Create JSON module, or escape the text before mapping it in.

/blog/zapier-social-media-automation.html:
Zapier social media automation: one Zap, every network

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-11-26 · 7 min read

Zapier connects to almost everything, but posting to TikTok, Threads or Bluesky, or scheduling for later, needs more than its built-in social apps. One Webhooks by Zapier step that calls a posting API handles all of it. Here is the Zap, step by step.

Short answer: use any trigger (a new Google Sheets row, a new RSS item, a form submission), then a Webhooks by Zapier → Custom Request step that sends the post to one publishing API. The API posts or schedules it to every network you connected, so one Zap covers X, LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Threads, Bluesky, Facebook and Pinterest.

Know this first: Webhooks is a premium app Zapier lists Webhooks by Zapier as a premium app, so a Zap that uses it needs a paid Zapier plan (new accounts get a trial). If you need this on a free tool, Make and n8n can do the same with their HTTP modules.

Why not use Zapier's built-in social apps?

Zapier has apps for some networks, such as LinkedIn and Facebook Pages. They're fine for one network, but each is a separate connection and action, coverage of newer networks like Threads and Bluesky is thin, and most post immediately rather than at a chosen time. Sending everything through one posting API keeps the Zap to two steps and gives you scheduling.

Step 1: API key and account IDs

  1. In Social0, connect your networks under Connections, then create an API key under Developer → API keys (sk_live_…, shown once).
  2. Run this once in a terminal, or in a test Webhooks by Zapier → GET step, and copy the id of each account you want to post to:
curl -s https://api.social0.app/v1/accounts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_YOUR_KEY"

Step 2: the posting step

Add an action: Webhooks by Zapier → Custom Request. Use Custom Request rather than POST, because POST's form fields make it awkward to send a list of account IDs.

Method:   POST
URL:      https://api.social0.app/v1/posts/schedule
Headers:  Authorization | Bearer sk_live_…
          Content-Type  | application/json
Data:
{
  "content": "(map your text field here)",
  "platforms": ["ACCOUNT_ID_1", "ACCOUNT_ID_2"],
  "scheduledAt": "(map your date field here)"
}
  • Post now instead: use /v1/posts/publish and remove scheduledAt.
  • Dates: use a Formatter by Zapier → Date / Time step to turn your sheet's date into an ISO time like 2026-12-01T09:00:00Z. Or send your local time followed by +default (e.g. 2026-12-01T09:00:00+default) to use the time zone in your Social0 settings.
  • Quotes in your text break raw JSON. Run the text through a Formatter → Text → Replace step to escape double quotes, or keep post text free of them.

Step 3: pick a trigger

  • Google Sheets → New or Updated Spreadsheet Row: a content calendar anyone on the team can fill in. Add a final Update Spreadsheet Row step that marks the row as scheduled. The content calendar guide has a column layout.
  • RSS by Zapier → New Item in Feed: announce every new blog post or changelog entry. Add an AI step to turn the title and summary into a short post.
  • Forms, Airtable or Notion: collect post ideas from your team and post the approved ones.

Step 4: hear about failures

The API accepts the post right away (a 202 with status: "queued") and publishes in the background, so a green Zap run doesn't mean the post is live. Make a second Zap with Webhooks by Zapier → Catch Hook, register its URL in Social0 for post.failed, and send the details to Slack or email. Why scheduled posts fail covers the usual reasons.

Images and video

Media needs three requests: POST /v1/media/presign, an upload of the file to the returned URL, and POST /v1/media/confirm, which returns a media ID for the post's media array. That's easier in a code step or in n8n than in plain Zapier steps, so many people keep Zapier for text and link posts and add media in the dashboard.

Post to 9 networks from one Zap. The API is on every Social0 plan, including Free. See the Social0 API

Frequently asked questions

Can Zapier post to social media automatically?

Yes. Zapier has apps for some networks, and a Webhooks by Zapier step can call a posting API like Social0's to publish or schedule to many networks from one Zap.

Is Webhooks by Zapier free?

No. Zapier lists it as a premium app, so the Zap needs a paid Zapier plan after any trial. Make and n8n offer HTTP modules on their free tiers.

Can Zapier schedule posts for a specific time?

Yes, if the step calls an endpoint that accepts a future time, such as Social0's /v1/posts/schedule with scheduledAt. You can also hold a Zap with Delay by Zapier, but sending the time to the API is simpler.

Can Zapier post to TikTok, Threads and Bluesky?

Through a posting API, yes. The same request that posts to LinkedIn or X also posts to TikTok, Threads and Bluesky when those accounts are connected in Social0.

Why use Custom Request instead of POST in Webhooks by Zapier?

Custom Request lets you send raw JSON, including the list of account IDs. The POST action builds the body from form fields, which makes lists awkward.

/blog/n8n-social-media-automation.html:
n8n social media automation: post everywhere from one workflow

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-11-26 · 9 min read

n8n can post to social media, but wiring X, LinkedIn, Instagram and TikTok separately means four developer apps and four sets of quirks. Here is a workflow that posts to all of them with one HTTP Request node, with copy-paste settings.

Short answer: n8n is great at the trigger and the content (a schedule, a Google Sheet, an RSS feed, an AI step). The hard part is publishing: each network needs its own developer app, OAuth setup and media rules. The simplest pattern is to let n8n build the post and send it to one publishing API with an HTTP Request node, which then posts to every network you connected.

This guide builds that workflow with Social0's API, step by step. The same shape works with any unified posting API.

Why not use n8n's built-in social nodes?

n8n ships nodes for some networks, such as X and LinkedIn. They work, but each one needs credentials from that network's own developer program, and you build and maintain a separate branch per network. Coverage is uneven: TikTok, Threads and Bluesky publishing usually mean raw API calls, and Instagram means the Graph API with its container-then-publish flow. The posting API guide covers what each network asks for.

Two ways to post from n8n
One node per networkOne publishing API
Developer apps to set upOne per networkNone (connect accounts in the dashboard)
Nodes in the workflowOne branch per networkOne HTTP Request node
TikTok, Threads, BlueskyCustom API callsSame request as every other network
SchedulingWait node or your own queueA scheduledAt field
FailuresHandled per branchOne status per network, plus webhooks

Step 1: connect accounts and create an API key

  1. In Social0, connect the networks you want under Connections. OAuth stays in the dashboard; n8n never sees your social passwords.
  2. Open Developer → API keys, create a key, and copy the sk_live_… value (it's shown once).
  3. In n8n, create a credential of type Header Auth: name Authorization, value Bearer sk_live_….

Step 2: get your account IDs

Posts target account IDs, not network names. Add a temporary HTTP Request node, run it once, and copy the id of each account you want to post to:

Method:          GET
URL:             https://api.social0.app/v1/accounts
Authentication:  Generic Credential Type → Header Auth (the credential from step 1)

Step 3: the publish node

This one node does the posting. Set it up like this:

Method:          POST
URL:             https://api.social0.app/v1/posts/schedule
Authentication:  Header Auth (same credential)
Send Body:       JSON
Body:
{
  "content": "{{ $json.text }}",
  "platforms": ["ACCOUNT_ID_1", "ACCOUNT_ID_2"],
  "scheduledAt": "{{ $json.publishAt }}"
}
  • Publish now instead of scheduling: use /v1/posts/publish and drop scheduledAt.
  • Time format: scheduledAt takes an ISO time such as 2026-12-01T09:00:00Z, an explicit offset like +05:30, or +default to use the time zone set in your Social0 settings. It must be in the future and within a year.
  • No double posts on retries: on the publish endpoint, add an Idempotency-Key header that is unique per post, such as the sheet row ID; a retry with the same key gets the original response back instead of a second post. For scheduled posts, mark the row as done right after the node succeeds (step 4) so the next run skips it.
Publish returns before the post is live A publish call answers 202 with status: "queued": the job was accepted, not finished. To act on the result, either poll GET /v1/jobs/{tracking_id} or, better, let Social0 call you back with a webhook (step 5).

Step 4: pick a trigger

Put one of these in front of the publish node. Each one only has to output text (and publishAt if you're scheduling):

  • Google Sheets content calendar: a Schedule Trigger every hour → Google Sheets (read rows where Status is "ready") → publish → Google Sheets (set Status to "scheduled"). Writers fill in a sheet; n8n does the rest. The content calendar guide has a column layout that works.
  • Blog or changelog to social: an RSS Feed Trigger on your blog → an AI step that writes a short post from the title and summary → publish. Every new article gets announced automatically.
  • AI-written posts with review: an AI step drafts the post → n8n sends it to Slack or email for approval → on approval, publish. Keep a human in the loop for anything public.

Step 5: know when a post fails

Add a Webhook node in a second workflow and register its URL in Social0 for the post.published and post.failed events. Social0 then calls n8n when each post finishes, with a per-network status. Send failures to Slack so a rejected video or an expired login doesn't go unnoticed. Every delivery is signed in the X-Social0-Signature header, so you can check it really came from Social0. Why scheduled posts fail covers the usual causes.

Adding images and video

Media is three calls: ask for an upload URL (POST /v1/media/presign), upload the file to that URL with an HTTP PUT, then confirm it (POST /v1/media/confirm) to get a media ID. Put the ID in a media array on the post. In n8n that is three HTTP Request nodes in a row. Images can be up to about 50 MB and videos about 500 MB, and the file must match each network's specs: see the video specs guide.

Limits to plan around

  • API rate limits are per hour and depend on your plan (the free plan allows 60 requests an hour), which is plenty for a posting workflow that runs every hour.
  • Platform rules still apply: Instagram's 5-hashtag cap, X's 280 characters, TikTok's privacy rules. Check copy with the free post previews before you automate it.
  • Write different text per network when it matters. One message cross-posted everywhere is fine for announcements; cross-posting vs repurposing covers when to rewrite.

Get an API key and post to 9 networks from n8n. Free plan includes the API, no credit card. See the Social0 API

Frequently asked questions

Can n8n post to social media automatically?

Yes. Use a trigger (Schedule, Google Sheets, RSS or a webhook), build the post text, and send it to a publishing API with an HTTP Request node, or use n8n's own nodes for each network.

Can n8n post to Instagram and TikTok?

Not with a simple built-in node for every case. Instagram needs the Graph API's two-step container flow, and TikTok needs an approved Content Posting API app. A unified API like Social0 handles both through the same HTTP Request node.

How do I schedule posts from n8n?

Either hold the item with a Wait node until the time comes, or send it straight away to an API that accepts a future time. Social0's /v1/posts/schedule takes a scheduledAt field up to a year ahead, so n8n doesn't need to stay running until then.

How do I stop n8n from posting twice?

For immediate posts, send an Idempotency-Key header that is unique per post, such as the spreadsheet row ID; a retry within 24 hours gets the original response instead of a duplicate. For scheduled posts, mark the row as scheduled as soon as the request succeeds so the next run skips it.

Do I need a paid plan to use the Social0 API from n8n?

No. The API is on every plan, including Free (3 accounts, 10 posts). Paid plans raise the post and account limits and the hourly API quota.

/blog/post-to-social-media-from-claude-c.html:
Post to social media from Claude Code

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-11-26 · 7 min read

You already ship from Claude Code. It can also write the launch post, turn the changelog into a thread, and schedule both to X, LinkedIn, Threads and Bluesky, without leaving the terminal. Here is the setup, two ways, and the prompts that work.

Short answer: install the social0 CLI, log in with an API key, and tell Claude Code it can use it. Claude Code has a shell, so a CLI is the simplest tool for it: it runs social0 schedule … like any other command. If you prefer MCP, add Social0's hosted MCP server with one claude mcp add command instead.

This is the developer version of posting from ChatGPT or Claude. The difference is context: Claude Code can read your git log, diff and changelog, so it writes posts about what you actually shipped.

Option A: the CLI (recommended)

  1. Connect your accounts in Social0 under Connections (OAuth stays in the dashboard).
  2. Create an API key under Developer → API keys.
  3. Install and log in:
npm install -g social0
social0 login        # paste sk_live_… (input is masked)
social0 accounts     # lists your connected accounts with short IDs

That's all the setup. Claude Code can now run commands like these when you ask it to:

social0 publish -c "v2.3 is out: faster exports and dark mode" -p twitter linkedin
social0 schedule -c "Launch day tomorrow" -p twitter threads bluesky -t "tomorrow 9am"
social0 upload ./screenshot.png --json   # returns a media ID to attach with -m

Times like tomorrow 9am, next monday or in 2 hours use your local time. The CLI page has every command.

Tell Claude Code how you post

Add a few lines to your project's CLAUDE.md so every session knows the rules without you repeating them:

## Social posts
- Use the `social0` CLI to post. Run `social0 accounts` first.
- Never publish without showing me the exact text first.
- Default: schedule with `-t`, don't publish immediately.
- X max 280 chars; LinkedIn can be longer; no hashtags on X.

Option B: MCP

If you'd rather Claude Code use structured tools than shell commands, add Social0's hosted MCP server:

claude mcp add --transport http social0 https://mcp.social0.app/mcp

Then run /mcp inside Claude Code and sign in to Social0 when the browser opens. No API key goes in a config file; the sign-in creates a key you can revoke in the dashboard. Ask "show my connected Social0 accounts" to check it works.

CLI or MCP in Claude Code?
CLIMCP
Setupnpm install + API keyOne claude mcp add + browser sign-in
Local files (screenshots, videos)Upload straight from diskPass a public URL or base64 data
Also works in CI and scriptsYes, same commandsNo
Best forDevelopers who live in the terminalStructured tools, no global install

Prompts that work

  • "Read the commits since the last tag and write a 4-post X thread about what changed for users. Show me, then schedule it for tomorrow 9am."
  • "Turn CHANGELOG.md's newest entry into a LinkedIn post and a short X post. Schedule LinkedIn for Tuesday 10am and X for Tuesday 4pm."
  • "Upload docs/settings.png and draft a post announcing the new settings page on Threads and Bluesky. Show me before scheduling."
  • "How did my X and Bluesky posts do over the last 28 days?" (runs social0 analytics --range 28d; live analytics cover X, Bluesky, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest today)
Keep a human in the loop Posting is public and hard to take back. Have Claude Code show the exact text and the target accounts before it runs the command, and default to scheduling, so you have time to cancel. The CLAUDE.md snippet above makes that the rule for every session.

From Claude Code to CI

Once a prompt works well, you can make it automatic. The CLI reads SOCIAL0_API_KEY from the environment, so the same social0 publish command runs in a GitHub Action on every release. Social media automation for developers covers release pipelines and webhooks, and the n8n guide covers no-code workflows.

Install the CLI and let Claude Code post your launches. Free plan includes the CLI, API and MCP. Use Social0 with Claude

Frequently asked questions

Can Claude Code post to social media?

Yes. Give it a tool to call: a CLI such as social0, which it runs in its shell, or an MCP server added with claude mcp add. It can then publish or schedule posts to the accounts you connected.

Should I use the CLI or MCP with Claude Code?

Claude Code has a shell, so the CLI is the simplest option and handles local files directly. MCP is a good fit if you want structured tools without installing a global npm package.

Which networks can Claude Code post to through Social0?

X, LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Threads, Bluesky, Facebook and Pinterest, as long as the account is connected in Social0.

Is it safe to give Claude Code access to my social accounts?

It never sees your social passwords: accounts are connected in the Social0 dashboard, and Claude Code only gets an API key you can revoke at any time. Add a CLAUDE.md rule that it must show you the post before publishing.

Can Claude Code schedule posts for later?

Yes. With the CLI, use social0 schedule with -t and a time such as "tomorrow 9am". Through MCP, ask it to schedule for a date and time.

/blog/how-to-schedule-x-posts.html:
How to schedule posts on X (tweets and threads)

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-11-26 · 7 min read

X has a built-in scheduler on the web, and it is starting to reach the iPhone app. It handles single posts well and threads badly. Here is the native flow, where your scheduled posts hide, and when a scheduler is the better route.

Short answer: on x.com, write your post, click the calendar-and-clock icon under the text box, pick a date and time, click Confirm, then Schedule. It is free and works for any account. To see what's queued, open the same icon and choose Scheduled posts.

Schedule a post on x.com

  1. Open x.com in a desktop or mobile browser and click Post (or use the box at the top of your home timeline).
  2. Write the post and add images, a video or a GIF.
  3. Click the schedule icon (a calendar with a clock) in the row of icons under the text.
  4. Pick the date, time and time zone, and click Confirm.
  5. The Post button changes to Schedule. Click it.

The date picker goes well over a year ahead, so the window is not the problem; remembering what you queued is.

Where scheduled posts hide

Scheduled posts don't appear on your profile or in the app's drafts. On x.com, open the composer, click the schedule icon, and choose Scheduled posts (some layouts call this Unsent posts). From there you can open a post to edit it, change its time, or delete it.

Can you schedule on the X mobile app?

For years the answer was no. In September 2026 X began rolling scheduling out in the iPhone app, but not to every account, and reports at the time found no sign of it on Android. How to schedule YouTube videos and Shorts

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-11-26 · 7 min read

YouTube's own scheduler is good: it works on desktop and in the app, for long videos and Shorts. Here is how to use it, how to change a scheduled time, the catches nobody mentions, and when a cross-platform scheduler is worth it.

Short answer: upload in YouTube Studio, and on the Visibility step choose Schedule instead of Public. Pick a date, time and time zone, then click Schedule. The video stays private until that moment and then goes public on its own. Shorts work the same way, on desktop or in the YouTube app.

Unlike TikTok's, YouTube's native scheduler is solid. The main reason to use another tool is when the same vertical clip also needs to go to TikTok, Instagram Reels and the rest at the same time.

Schedule a video in YouTube Studio (desktop)

  1. Go to studio.youtube.com and click Create → Upload videos.
  2. Pick the file. While it uploads, fill in the title (up to 100 characters), description, thumbnail and audience setting.
  3. Click through Video elements (end screens, cards) and Checks (copyright and ad suitability).
  4. On Visibility, choose Schedule, then set the date, time and time zone.
  5. Click Schedule. The video appears in your Content list with a clock icon until it publishes.
Let the checks finish first If you schedule a video for the next hour and the copyright check is still running, a claim can land after it is already public. For anything time-sensitive, upload a day early and schedule it, so the checks and HD processing are done well before it goes live.

Schedule a Short or video in the YouTube app

  1. Tap + (Create) and choose Short or Upload a video.
  2. Record or pick the clip, edit it, and tap Next.
  3. On the details screen, tap Visibility and choose Schedule.
  4. Set the date and time (check AM and PM), go back, and tap Upload.

YouTube treats a video as a Short when it is vertical or square and up to 3 minutes long. You do not choose "Short" in Studio; YouTube classifies it from the file. If a clip you meant as a Short shows up as a regular video, the aspect ratio or length is usually why. The free video resizer converts a landscape clip to 9:16 in your browser.

Change or cancel a scheduled video

  • New time: open the video from Content, click the visibility setting, and pick a new date and time under Schedule.
  • Publish now: in the same place, switch visibility to Public.
  • Cancel: switch it to Private. The video stays in your channel, unpublished.

Premieres: scheduling with a live countdown

A Premiere is a scheduled video that plays for everyone at the same time, with a watch page and live chat that open before it starts. Choose Schedule, then tick Set as Premiere. It works well for launches and trailers; for a regular weekly upload, a normal schedule is simpler.

Gotchas worth knowing

  • The date under the video is Pacific Time. YouTube shows the publish date in PT, so a video scheduled for 9am in India appears dated the previous evening in the US. If the date matters, schedule it in PT.
  • A strike pauses your schedule. During a Community Guidelines strike penalty, scheduled videos do not publish. They stay private, and you have to reschedule them when the penalty ends.
  • Subscribers get notified at publish time, not at upload time. That is the point of scheduling: pick the hour your audience is online, not the hour you finished editing.

Scheduling Shorts alongside TikTok and Reels

If you make vertical video, the same clip usually goes to YouTube Shorts, TikTok and Instagram Reels. Doing that natively means three uploads, three captions and three schedulers. Reels vs TikTok vs Shorts covers how each one ranks the same clip.

In Social0 you upload once and select YouTube with the other accounts. Set a YouTube title (up to 100 characters); the caption becomes the description. Social0 classifies Shorts from duration and aspect ratio, and the post goes on the same calendar as your Reels and TikToks. Studio-only features such as end screens, playlists and unlisted visibility stay in YouTube Studio.

Upload once, schedule Shorts, TikTok and Reels together. Free plan, no credit card. See the YouTube scheduler

Start from the platform defaults in the best time to post guide. Then open Analytics → Audience in YouTube Studio: the "When your viewers are on YouTube" chart shows the hours your own viewers are active. Scheduling one to two hours before the peak gives the video time to pick up its first views.

Open the video from the Content page in YouTube Studio, click its visibility setting, and pick a new date and time under Schedule. To publish it immediately, switch visibility to Public.

The most common reasons are an active Community Guidelines strike, which pauses scheduled uploads, or a video that was never fully processed. Check the video's status on the Content page and reschedule it.

Scheduling sets a video to go public at a chosen time. For an unlisted video, upload it as unlisted and change the visibility yourself when you are ready.

No. A scheduled video is published the same way as one made public by hand, and subscribers are notified at the publish time. Scheduling helps when it lets you publish at the hour your viewers are online.

/blog/instagram-hashtag-limit.html:
Instagram's 5-hashtag limit: what changed and what works now

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-09-20 · 8 min read

Thirty hashtags became five in December 2025, and it is enforced at publish time — not a suggestion. Here is what the cap covers, why Instagram made the change, and how to choose five tags that do real work.

On 19 December 2025, Instagram announced that every feed post and Reel is capped at five hashtags. The previous limit was thirty. This was confirmed by Instagram's own Creators account and by Adam Mosseri, and it is enforced at publish time rather than being advisory.

If your workflow involved a saved block of twenty-five tags pasted into a first comment, that workflow no longer runs.

What the cap actually covers

  • Feed posts and Reels, both capped at five.
  • Caption and comments together. Moving tags into a first comment does not buy you extra — the old standard workaround is closed.
  • Enforced, not ignored. Exceeding it means the post is blocked or the extra tags are stripped, depending on surface. You do not get a silent pass.
If you publish through an API This is a validation rule, not a style guide. A scheduler or integration that still sends thirty tags will start producing publish failures or silently truncated captions. Anything you built against the old limit needs its validation updated.

Why Instagram did it

The stated reason is content quality: long tag lists were mostly irrelevant to the post and used to game discovery, which made the signal worse for everyone. The more useful read is strategic — Instagram is becoming a search engine, and hashtags were getting in the way.

Discovery on Instagram now leans on the platform understanding your content directly: it reads your caption, analyses your image and video, and matches all of that against what people type into search. In that world, thirty generic tags are noise that makes classification harder, not easier. Five precise ones are a useful hint.

What hashtags do now

The honest framing: hashtags are categorisation signals, not distribution levers. They tell Instagram what your post is about so it can place you in the right topic neighbourhoods. They do not, by themselves, push your post to more people.

Old model (pre-2026)Current model
Tags were discovery surfaces people browsed.Tags are classification input for recommendations and search.
More tags = wider net.More tags = diluted signal (and now, a rejected post).
Mixing big and small tags was the standard play.Precision beats volume; a huge generic tag mostly wastes a slot.
Hashtags drove reach.Caption keywords and content quality drive reach; tags refine placement.

How to choose five

With five slots, each one should be doing a distinct job. A structure that works:

  1. One topic tag — what the post is actually about, specifically. #sourdoughstarter, not #food.
  2. One niche/community tag — where your people already gather. Smaller is better; a tag with 400k posts beats one with 40m.
  3. One audience or intent tag — who it is for or what they are trying to do. #firsttimefounder, #mealprepforone.
  4. One local or contextual tag — city, region, event, or season, if genuinely relevant. Local tags punch well above their size.
  5. One branded tag — yours. It compounds over time and makes your own archive searchable.

If a tag does not fit one of those jobs, leave the slot empty. Four good tags beat five where the fifth is #instagood.

The bigger lever is your caption Instagram matches search queries against captions, usernames, bios, and locations. A caption written in the words your audience would actually type now does more discovery work than the tags do. Write the first sentence for a human and the rest for search — in that order.

What this breaks in a cross-posting workflow

This change makes one caption for all networks meaningfully harder, because the hashtag conventions have now diverged sharply:

PlatformHashtag reality
InstagramHard cap of 5. Exceeding it fails or truncates.
TikTokStill genuinely useful for discovery. No comparable hard cap.
LinkedInAbout three is the convention; more reads as spam.
XLittle benefit. One or two at most.
BlueskyMinimal benefit; the feed is not tag-driven.
ThreadsSupports a single topic tag.
PinterestDescriptions are keyword-driven rather than tag-driven.

So a shared tag block is now actively harmful in both directions: too many for Instagram to accept, and mostly dead weight on X and Bluesky. This is exactly the case for per-platform caption overrides — one base caption, with the tag line adjusted where the network demands it.

Override the caption only on the networks that need different tags. See the Instagram scheduler

What to do this week

  1. Delete your saved hashtag block. It is now a liability, not an asset.
  2. Audit scheduled posts. Anything queued with more than five tags will fail or be trimmed when it fires. Fix them before they go out.
  3. Update any API validation you own to reject more than five before upload rather than discovering it from a platform error.
  4. Rewrite captions for search, using the phrasing your audience would type.
  5. Build a small tag library — five to ten per content pillar — and pick from it rather than reusing one universal set.

The change is less painful than it first looks. The thirty-tag block was never producing much value; it just felt like effort. Five deliberate tags plus a caption written for search is both less work and better aligned with how Instagram now finds things.

Frequently asked questions

Five per feed post or Reel. Instagram announced the change on 19 December 2025, reducing the limit from thirty. It is enforced at publish time — exceeding it blocks the post or strips the extra tags.

No. The cap applies to the caption and comments together, which closes the standard workaround. Five is the total across both.

Do hashtags still work on Instagram?

Yes, but as categorisation signals rather than distribution levers. They help Instagram understand what your post is about so it can place it in the right recommendations and search results. They no longer push your post to a wider audience on their own.

Why did Instagram reduce the hashtag limit to 5?

Officially, to cut down on irrelevant tags used to game discovery. Strategically, Instagram is shifting toward search: it reads captions, images, and video directly to classify content, and long generic tag lists made that classification worse rather than better.

What happens to scheduled posts that already have 30 hashtags?

They will fail to publish or have the extra tags stripped when they fire, depending on the surface. Audit anything already queued and trim it to five before it goes out.

How the Instagram algorithm works in 2026

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-09-20 · 10 min read

There isn't one Instagram algorithm — there are four, and they rank on different things. Here's what each surface rewards, why a DM share is worth more than a like, and the reposting rule that quietly kills accounts.

The most common mistake in Instagram advice is talking about “the algorithm” as one system. Instagram runs separate ranking systems for Feed, Reels, Stories, and Explore, and they weight signals differently. Content that thrives in Explore can do nothing in Feed, and the reason is structural rather than mysterious.

Four surfaces, four sets of priorities

SurfaceRanks mainly onWhat that means for you
FeedRelationship strength, then interestReaches people who already interact with you. Good for conversion, poor for growth.
ReelsWatch time and sendsThe growth surface. Followers matter far less than whether the video holds and travels.
StoriesRecency and viewing historyAlmost purely your existing audience. A retention and relationship surface.
ExploreEngagement velocity and interest matchPure discovery. Fast early engagement is what gets you in.
The practical consequence If your goal is reach, you are making Reels. If your goal is converting people who already follow you, you are posting to Feed and Stories. Judging a Feed post by its reach, or a Story by its like count, is measuring the wrong thing.

The three signals Instagram has actually named

Adam Mosseri has repeatedly pointed at three, and they are worth taking literally because they are unusually specific:

  1. Watch time — how long people stay with your content.
  2. Sends per reach — how often someone forwards it in a DM, relative to how many saw it.
  3. Likes per reach — the weakest of the three, and the one everyone optimises for.

Note the *per reach* construction on two of them. These are rates, not totals. A post seen by 500 people with 50 sends outranks one seen by 50,000 with 200 sends. This is why small accounts can still break out, and why buying reach does not help.

Sends are the whole game

If you optimise for one thing on Instagram in 2026, make it sends — someone forwarding your post to a specific person in a DM. It is the most heavily weighted distribution signal for Reels, and it is qualitatively different from a like.

A like is a reflex. A send requires someone to think of a particular person and decide this is worth their attention. That is a much stronger relevance signal, and Instagram treats it accordingly.

Content people actually send:

  • “This is so you.” Content that describes a recognisable person or situation.
  • Genuinely useful and specific. A method, a spec, a fix worth passing to a colleague.
  • Funny in a targeted way. Broad humour gets liked; niche humour gets sent.
  • Something to react to together. A take someone wants a friend's opinion on.

What does not get sent: generic motivation, company announcements, and anything that reads as an ad. These can still get likes, which is why like-count optimisation quietly misleads you.

The repost rule

This one removes accounts from recommendations Original content receives substantially more distribution than reposted content — figures around 40–60% more are widely reported. More seriously, accounts posting roughly 10 or more reposts within 30 days can be excluded from recommendations entirely. Not down-ranked. Excluded.

This is the single most dangerous thing in this guide for anyone running an aggregator, a meme page, or a brand account that leans on user-generated content. The threshold is low enough to hit by accident.

What counts against you is reposting other people's content as your own. What is fine: your own content, genuine collaborations, and properly credited UGC where you have added something. If reposting is core to your account, the honest answer is that Instagram has decided against that model.

This also has a cross-posting implication. A video downloaded from TikTok with a visible watermark reads as unoriginal to exactly this system — which is the mechanism behind the watermark penalty covered in cross-posting vs repurposing.

What changed recently

  • Hashtags capped at five. Down from thirty, since December 2025, and enforced at publish time. Covered in full in Instagram's 5-hashtag limit.
  • Longer Reels are being recommended more. Instagram has been pushing longer storytelling into Explore, softening the old assumption that shorter always wins.
  • Automatic caption and audio translation. Reels now reach international audiences without you doing anything, which makes clear, plainly-worded captions more valuable.
  • Search matters more. Instagram matches queries against captions, bios, and usernames. Writing captions in the words people actually type is now a real discovery lever — arguably more than hashtags.

The soft limits worth knowing

ThresholdWhat happens
Reels over ~3 minutesAccepted, but Instagram stops pushing them to non-followers. Treat 3 min as the real ceiling.
More than 5 hashtagsBlocked or stripped at publish time.
~10+ reposts in 30 daysRisk of exclusion from recommendations.
25 API posts per rolling 24hPublishing limit per account. See Instagram API rate limits.

Schedule Reels, carousels, and Stories alongside your other networks. See the Instagram scheduler

A working approach

  1. Make Reels for reach, carousels for saves, Stories for retention. Match the format to the surface you need.
  2. Write the first line for a send, not a like. Ask who the viewer would forward this to.
  3. Keep Reels under 3 minutes, and open with something that earns the next two seconds.
  4. Post original content. If you must repost, keep it well under the threshold and add something real.
  5. Write captions in plain search language, then five deliberate hashtags.
  6. Check sends and saves, not likes. They are in the post insights and they are what the ranking actually uses.

The theme across all four surfaces is that Instagram has moved from measuring approval to measuring attention and transmission. Likes are cheap and the system knows it.

Frequently asked questions

How does the Instagram algorithm work in 2026?

Instagram runs separate ranking systems for Feed, Reels, Stories, and Explore. Feed ranks mainly on relationship strength, Reels on watch time and sends, Stories on recency, and Explore on engagement velocity. The three signals Instagram has named directly are watch time, sends per reach, and likes per reach.

What is the most important Instagram ranking signal?

Sends — someone forwarding your post to a specific person in a DM. It is the most heavily weighted distribution signal for Reels because it requires real intent, unlike a like. Watch time is a close second, and likes are the weakest of the three.

Does reposting content hurt your Instagram reach?

Yes, significantly. Original content receives substantially more distribution, and accounts posting roughly ten or more reposts within thirty days can be excluded from recommendations entirely. This also covers videos carrying another platform's watermark.

How long should Instagram Reels be?

Under three minutes. The API accepts up to twenty minutes, but past roughly three Instagram stops recommending the Reel to non-followers — it publishes fine and existing followers see it, but it is excluded from discovery. Instagram has recently been recommending longer storytelling Reels more, but three minutes remains the practical ceiling.

Do likes still matter on Instagram?

They count, but they are the weakest of the three named signals and they are measured as likes per reach rather than a total. Optimising for likes tends to produce broadly agreeable content that nobody forwards, which is exactly what the current ranking discounts.

/blog/tiktok-algorithm-guide.html:
How the TikTok algorithm works in 2026

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-09-20 · 9 min read

TikTok stopped counting views and started counting attention. Watch time per impression now drives distribution — which changes the optimal video length in a way most advice hasn't caught up with.

TikTok remains the one major platform where an account with no followers can reach a million people, because distribution is decided by the content rather than the audience. That has not changed. What has changed is *which* attention metric it optimises.

The test phase

Every upload goes to a small initial audience first — and notably, that test group still leans on your existing followers. TikTok watches what they do. Strong signals earn a wider push, then a wider one again. Weak signals and the video stops.

This is the part people get wrong about “followers don't matter on TikTok”. They matter less for *eventual* reach than anywhere else, but they are still the gate: a video your own audience abandons rarely escapes the test phase. Making content your existing followers finish is how you buy a ticket to everyone else.

The signal hierarchy

Roughly in order of weight, based on what TikTok and published analyses describe.
SignalWeightNotes
Watch time & completion rateDominant — commonly estimated at 40–50% of ranking weightThe single biggest factor by a wide margin.
ReplaysVery highA rewatch is the strongest possible attention signal.
SharesHighNow weighted above likes. Sends the video off-platform or to a friend.
SavesHighSignals lasting value. Also above likes.
CommentsModerateEspecially when you reply and start a thread.
LikesLowThe cheapest action, weighted accordingly.
Negative feedbackStrongly negative“Not interested”, skips, and reports suppress hard.
The change that matters most Watch time per impression has replaced raw view count as the primary signal. TikTok is no longer asking “how many people saw this?” but “how much attention did each impression produce?” Total views are now closer to an output than an input.

Why this makes longer videos viable

This is the counterintuitive part, and it contradicts a lot of still-circulating advice.

Under a pure *completion rate* model, short wins — a 15-second video is easier to finish than a 60-second one. But under watch time per impression, total seconds held matter. A 60-second video watched to 80% delivers 48 seconds of attention per impression. A 15-second video watched to 95% delivers 14. The longer video wins on distribution despite the worse completion rate.

VideoCompletionAttention per impressionDistribution
15 seconds95%~14 secondsLower
60 seconds80%~48 secondsHigher
60 seconds25%~15 secondsComparable to the 15s clip

The honest reading: make videos as long as you can hold attention, and not one second longer. Padding a video to 60 seconds collapses the retention curve and you end up worse off than the short version. The skill is earning the duration, not choosing it.

The first two seconds

Watch time in the opening moments is the strongest early predictor, because that is where most abandonment happens. Everything about the first frame is doing work:

  • Start mid-action. No logo, no “hey guys”, no throat-clearing. The first frame should already be the thing.
  • Put the premise on screen immediately. People decide whether this concerns them before they have processed any audio.
  • Avoid a slow visual ramp. A static opening frame reads as skippable.
  • Design for mute. Most first views have no sound. Burned-in captions are not optional.
Replays are the cheat code A rewatch counts the full duration again. Videos that loop cleanly — where the last frame flows into the first — or that contain a detail people go back for, can post watch-time rates above 100%. This is the most under-exploited mechanic on the platform.

What suppresses reach

  • Watermarks from other platforms. TikTok discounts content carrying another network's watermark, exactly as Meta does in reverse. Export clean masters.
  • Low resolution. TikTok's posting API expects vertical 9:16 at 720×1280 or better; below that gets rejected or looks poor enough to lose retention.
  • Negative feedback. “Not interested” and rapid skips suppress hard. Clickbait that does not deliver generates both.
  • Reposting without transformation. Aggregated content performs poorly and risks the account.

Where timing fits

Less than anywhere else. Because TikTok surfaces content well beyond the hour it was posted, and can resurface videos weeks later, posting time is the weakest lever in this guide. Evening windows perform somewhat better, but a good video posted at a mediocre hour will still find its audience.

What matters far more is consistency — a steady stream gives the algorithm more chances to find the one that breaks out. That is a scheduling problem more than a creative one: filming several videos in one session and spreading them across two weeks is more sustainable than trying to produce daily. Bulk video tools exist for exactly this.

Batch-upload videos and spread them across a schedule. See the TikTok scheduler

A working approach

  1. Open mid-action, with the premise visible in frame one and captions burned in.
  2. Run as long as you can genuinely hold, rather than cutting to a target length.
  3. Build in a reason to rewatch — a clean loop, or a detail that rewards a second pass.
  4. Optimise for shares and saves, which now outweigh likes.
  5. Reply to comments in the first hour to start threads.
  6. Post consistently and let volume do the searching. Timing is the least of your levers here.

TikTok is the most meritocratic of the major feeds and the least forgiving. Nobody can buy their way past a bad retention curve, and nobody's follower count protects them from one.

Frequently asked questions

How does the TikTok algorithm work in 2026?

Every video is shown to a small test audience first, weighted toward your existing followers. TikTok measures the response — primarily watch time and completion rate, which are estimated to carry 40–50% of the ranking weight — and expands distribution if the signals are strong.

What is the most important TikTok ranking signal?

Watch time, specifically watch time per impression, which has replaced raw view count as the primary signal. Replays count the full duration again and are the strongest single signal available. Shares and saves now outweigh likes.

How long should TikTok videos be in 2026?

As long as you can genuinely hold attention. Because ranking uses watch time per impression rather than completion rate alone, a 60-second video watched to 80% out-distributes a 15-second video watched to 95%. But padding collapses retention, so the length has to be earned.

Do followers matter on TikTok?

Less than on any other platform for eventual reach, but they still gate it. The initial test audience leans on your existing followers, so a video your own audience abandons rarely escapes that phase to reach anyone else.

Does posting time matter on TikTok?

Less than on any other network. TikTok surfaces content well beyond the hour it was posted and can resurface videos weeks later. Evening windows perform somewhat better, but consistency and retention matter far more than the timestamp.

/blog/x-algorithm-guide.html:
How the X (Twitter) algorithm works in 2026

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-09-20 · 9 min read

X publishes its ranking code, which makes it the least mysterious major feed. Replies dominate, the first half hour decides most of your reach, and putting a link in the post costs you a third of it.

X is unusual among major platforms in that its ranking algorithm is open source. You do not have to infer how it works from experiments — the broad shape is published, and it has held up.

How a feed gets built

For each For You session, X assembles a candidate pool — commonly around 1,500 posts — drawn from accounts you follow and from out-of-network content it predicts you will engage with. Those candidates are scored by a neural ranking model (the “Heavy Ranker”) that predicts how likely you are to take each possible action. The predictions are weighted and summed, and the feed is the result, ordered by score.

The important implication: the weights on those predicted actions are not equal. Optimising for the cheap ones is a losing strategy.

Replies dominate everything

The single most important number here A reply is worth roughly 27× a like in X's scoring. Not marginally more — an order of magnitude more. Everything else in this guide follows from that one ratio.

X is optimising for conversation, because conversation keeps people on the platform. A post with 40 replies and 100 likes will substantially out-distribute one with 5 replies and 1,000 likes.

What this changes in practice:

  • Write posts that are answerable. A complete, self-contained statement leaves nothing to say. A specific claim, an open question, or a genuine disagreement invites a response.
  • Reply to your own replies. Each exchange is another high-weight signal, and it pulls the other person back.
  • Take the mild position, not the safe one. Universal agreement produces likes. A defensible opinion people want to push back on produces replies.
  • Avoid engagement bait. “Reply with a 🔥” generates low-quality replies, and since March 2026 reply *quality* is itself a ranking input.

That last point is newer and worth knowing: X now treats reply quality as a direct signal, with Premium users able to downvote replies flagged as AI-generated, misleading, or spam. Farming shallow replies is no longer neutral — it can work against you.

The first 30 minutes

Engagement velocity matters more than eventual totals, and the opening window is decisive — roughly 70% of a post's eventual reach is determined in the first half hour.

X's content also decays faster than any other network in this series. A post is largely finished within hours, where a Short can accumulate views for months. That makes timing matter more here than almost anywhere else.

  • Post when your audience is awake and scrolling. For most audiences that is weekday mornings, roughly 9am–12pm.
  • Be available for that half hour. Replying quickly compounds: your reply is a high-weight signal and it brings the replier back.
  • Do not post and leave. If you cannot attend the window, schedule it for when you can. That is the practical argument for scheduling on X — choosing a slot you can staff, not automating away your presence.

Links cost you reach

Posts containing an external link receive materially less distribution — figures around 30–40% less are commonly reported. X, like LinkedIn, would rather you stayed.

The workaround is the same and it still works: publish the post without the link, then put the link in your own reply. You keep the distribution on the main post and the people who want the link still get it.

Cross-posting note This is the opposite of Bluesky, which applies no link penalty at all. If you mirror posts between the two, the link belongs in the post on Bluesky and in a reply on X. See Bluesky vs Threads.

Premium changes the maths

Worth being plain about: Premium subscribers receive a reach multiplier — commonly described as 2–4× — and Premium replies are prioritised toward the top of conversation threads.

Whether that is good for the platform is a separate question. Operationally, if X is a meaningful channel for you, the subscription is doing more work than most of the tactics in this guide. Premium also raises the character limit from 280 to 25,000, which changes what you can publish — a scheduler needs to detect the account's actual status rather than assume 280.

Signal weights, roughly

ActionRelative weightNotes
ReplyHighest — ~27× a likeThe dominant signal.
BookmarkHighStrong private-value signal.
RepostHighExtends into a new network.
Profile click → engagementHighSignals genuine interest in you.
LikeBaselineCheap, and weighted as such.
“Not interested” / mute / blockStrongly negativeCosts far more than a like gains.

Threads, and why they work

A thread performs well for structural reasons rather than because X favours the format: each post is another surface, people replying to any post in the chain feeds the whole thing, and dwell time rises as people read down.

The first post still has to stand alone — nobody reaches post four if post one does not earn it. Write it as if it is the only thing that will be read, because for most of your audience it is.

Compose threads for X, Bluesky, and Threads from one draft. See the X scheduler

A working approach

  1. Write for replies. Every post should leave something worth saying.
  2. Post weekday mornings and stay for the first 30 minutes.
  3. Keep links out of the post. Put them in your own reply.
  4. Reply substantively to others daily. With replies weighted this heavily, being present in other people's threads is a genuine distribution strategy.
  5. Use threads for anything with more than one idea in it.
  6. Consider Premium if X matters commercially. The multiplier outweighs most tactical tuning.

X rewards being a participant rather than a broadcaster, and the 27× ratio is the platform stating that outright. An account that only posts is playing the weakest hand available.

Frequently asked questions

How does the X (Twitter) algorithm work in 2026?

X assembles a candidate pool of roughly 1,500 posts per session from in-network and out-of-network sources, scores each with a neural ranking model that predicts your likely actions, and orders the feed by weighted score. The algorithm is open source, so the broad structure is published rather than inferred.

What is the most important ranking signal on X?

Replies, by a wide margin — a reply is worth roughly 27 times a like in X's scoring. Bookmarks and reposts follow. Likes are the baseline and weighted accordingly, which is why posts with strong reply counts out-distribute posts with far more likes.

Do links reduce reach on X?

Yes, by around 30–40%. The standard workaround still works: publish the post without the link and add the link in your own reply. Note this is the opposite of Bluesky, which applies no link penalty.

How long does a post on X keep getting reach?

Not long — X decays faster than any other major network. Roughly 70% of a post's eventual reach is determined in the first 30 minutes, and a post is largely finished within hours. This makes posting time and being present to reply matter more on X than elsewhere.

Does X Premium actually increase reach?

Yes. Premium accounts receive a reach multiplier commonly described as 2–4×, and Premium replies are prioritised in conversation threads. It also raises the character limit from 280 to 25,000. If X is a commercially meaningful channel, the subscription tends to outweigh most tactical optimisation.

/blog/linkedin-algorithm-guide.html:
How the LinkedIn algorithm works in 2026

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-09-20 · 10 min read

Dwell time overtook likes, the first hour decides everything, and company pages are structurally disadvantaged. What the algorithm rewards now, and which once-reliable tactics are dead.

LinkedIn is the one major network where organic reach for a small account is still genuinely achievable. It is also the one where the advice ages fastest — most of what worked in 2023 has been actively neutralised.

Here is the current shape of it.

The first hour decides the post

When you publish, LinkedIn shows the post to a small slice of your network — commonly cited as 2–5%. It watches what happens. Strong early signals earn expansion to second- and third-degree connections; weak ones mean the post effectively stops there.

The practical consequences are unglamorous but real:

  • Post when your audience is actually online. For most B2B audiences that is Tuesday to Thursday, roughly 7:30–9:00am — people checking LinkedIn before the day starts.
  • Be present for the first hour. Replying to comments quickly is itself a ranking signal, and it pulls the commenter back for another interaction.
  • Do not publish and leave. A post you cannot tend for an hour is better scheduled for a time you can.
Why this makes scheduling useful, not useless The instinct is that automation conflicts with being present. The opposite: scheduling lets you choose a slot you know you can attend, instead of posting whenever you happened to finish writing. Write on Sunday, publish Tuesday 8am, be there for the hour.

Dwell time is the dominant signal

The single most important shift: LinkedIn now weights how long people spend with your post above how many liked it. A post that stops the scroll for twenty seconds outperforms one that collects quick likes as people pass.

What this rewards:

  • Posts worth reading to the end. 150–300 words is the sweet spot — enough substance to hold attention, short enough to finish.
  • A first two lines that earn the “see more” click. Expanding the post is itself a dwell signal, so the opening is doing double duty.
  • Documents and carousels, which generate far more dwell time than a single image because people swipe through them.
  • Specifics over abstractions. Numbers, named situations, and real detail hold attention; generic insight does not.

And what it punishes: anything that looks like it was written to be skimmed. The one-line-per-paragraph broetry format that dominated 2022 now reads as a tell, and it gives people less to spend time on.

Format, ranked

FormatReachWhy
Text-onlyHighestNo competing element, no outbound link, pure dwell time. Still the most reliable format.
Document / carouselHigh2–3x the dwell time of a single image. Excellent for frameworks and step-by-step content.
Native video (under ~30s)High for cold audiencesStrong completion rates. Longer video drops off sharply.
Single imageModerateFine, but the image has to add something the text does not.
Post with an outbound linkLowestLinkedIn suppresses content that sends people away. Put the link in the first comment.
The link workaround still works Publish the post without a link, then add the link as your own first comment and edit it into the post later if you want. The reach difference is large enough to be worth the extra step.

Personal profiles beat company pages, structurally

This is not a tactic gap you can close with better content. Company page organic posts make up a very small share of what appears in feeds — figures around 2% are commonly cited — while personal profiles see several times the engagement for equivalent content.

LinkedIn is a network of people, and it ranks accordingly. What to do about it:

  1. Publish the substance from personal profiles — founders, engineers, whoever has something specific to say.
  2. Use the company page for record, not reach. Announcements, credibility for people who look you up, and a home for the brand.
  3. Do not have the page post and the team mechanically reshare it. Resharing a page post carries the page post's weak distribution. Writing an original take performs far better.
  4. Give people their own angle. Five people posting the same launch in their own words beats one page post with five reshares.

If you are coordinating several people posting on the same theme, that is a scheduling problem — staggering posts across days so they do not compete with each other, and keeping track of who covered what. Social0's teams and workspaces handle multiple people publishing to their own connected accounts under one workflow.

Coordinate several people posting to their own LinkedIn profiles. See the LinkedIn scheduler

What stopped working

  • “Comment your email and I'll send the guide.” Heavily penalised. It generated comment volume without conversation, and the algorithm now recognises the pattern.
  • Engagement pods. LinkedIn detects coordinated reciprocal engagement and discounts it. At scale it risks the account.
  • Broetry formatting. One line per paragraph to force the “see more” click. Recognised, and it reduces the dwell time it was designed to manufacture.
  • Hashtag stuffing. Three relevant tags at most. LinkedIn never leaned on them heavily and leans less now.
  • Pure AI-written posts. Generic model output reads as generic and gets the engagement generic content deserves. The useful pattern is AI for structure and editing, with your own specifics and opinion carrying the post.

A cadence that works

  1. Three to four posts a week, from a personal profile. More is possible; fewer struggles to build momentum.
  2. Tuesday to Thursday, 7:30–9:00am, in your audience's timezone. Test around it, but start there.
  3. Rotate formats. Two text posts, one document, one video in a typical week.
  4. Block the first hour after publishing for replies. This is the highest-leverage hour you will spend on LinkedIn.
  5. Comment substantively on other people's posts daily. Reach on LinkedIn compounds through visibility in other people's comment sections more than most people expect.

None of this is a hack. The algorithm has converged on rewarding content people genuinely spend time with, written by a person with a name and a face, who then turns up to talk about it. That is harder to game and easier to sustain than what it replaced.

Frequently asked questions

How does the LinkedIn algorithm work in 2026?

LinkedIn shows a new post to a small slice of your network — around 2–5% — and watches the early response. Strong signals in roughly the first hour earn expansion to wider degrees of connection. Dwell time, meaning how long people spend reading, is now the dominant ranking signal, ahead of likes.

What type of LinkedIn post gets the most reach?

Text-only posts of roughly 150–300 words, followed by document or carousel posts, which generate two to three times the dwell time of a single image. Posts containing an outbound link get the least reach — put the link in the first comment instead.

Do LinkedIn company pages get less reach than personal profiles?

Yes, substantially and structurally. Company page posts make up a very small share of feed content, while personal profiles see several times the engagement for equivalent posts. Publish substance from personal profiles and use the page for announcements and credibility.

Should I put links in LinkedIn posts?

Not in the post body if reach matters. LinkedIn suppresses content that sends people off-platform. Publish without the link and add it as your own first comment — the reach difference is large enough to justify the extra step.

How often should I post on LinkedIn?

Three to four times a week from a personal profile, ideally Tuesday to Thursday between 7:30 and 9:00am in your audience's timezone. Consistency matters more than volume, and being available to reply during the first hour after posting is worth more than an extra post.

/blog/social-media-engagement-rate.html:
Engagement rate: formulas, benchmarks, and what to actually track

By Abhishek BR · Published 2026-09-20 · 9 min read

Three different formulas, all called “engagement rate”, all giving different answers for the same post. Here is how each one works, which to pick, and what a good number looks like per platform.

Engagement rate is the most quoted metric in social media and the least consistently defined. Two tools can report the same post as 1.2% and 6.5% and both be correct, because they are dividing by different things.

That matters when you are comparing yourself to a benchmark, or to last quarter, or to a competitor. Most of the time the comparison is meaningless because the denominators differ.

The three formulas

All three are legitimate. They answer different questions, and they are not comparable to each other.
FormulaCalculationAnswers
By reach (ERR)engagements ÷ reach × 100Of the people who actually saw this, how many acted? The best measure of content quality.
By followers (ER)engagements ÷ followers × 100How active is my audience relative to its size? The only one comparable across accounts.
By impressionsengagements ÷ impressions × 100Similar to reach but counts repeat views, so it always reads lower.
The one rule Pick one and never switch. A trend line built from mixed formulas is noise. If you change formula, recalculate your history or start a new chart — do not splice them.

Which one to pick

It depends on the decision you are making.

  • Judging content → by reach. It isolates the post from the size of your audience, so it tells you whether the content worked.
  • Reporting to a client or exec → by followers. It is the one competitors and benchmarks are usually quoted in, and it is the only one you can calculate for an account you do not own.
  • Diagnosing a drop → both. If reach-based holds steady while follower-based falls, your content is fine and distribution shrank. If reach-based falls, the content is the problem. That single comparison is the most useful diagnostic in social analytics.

What counts as an engagement

The other reason numbers disagree. There is no universal definition, and the choice materially changes the result.

  • Always counted: likes, comments, shares.
  • Usually counted: saves. Often the highest-intent action on Instagram and the strongest signal to the algorithm.
  • Sometimes counted: profile visits, link clicks, follows from the post, sticker taps.
  • Rarely counted, and shouldn't be: plain views or impressions. These are passive — folding them in inflates the number and hides what is happening.

Write your definition down. In six months you will not remember whether saves were in, and neither will whoever inherits the report.

2026 benchmarks

Treat these as orientation, not targets. They move with industry, account size, and which formula the study used — which is exactly the problem described above.

Follower-based rates from published 2026 studies. Sources differ substantially; the ranking is more reliable than the absolute numbers.
PlatformTypical rangeNotes
TikTok3–5%Consistently the highest. Distribution is content-led rather than follower-led.
LinkedIn2–6%High but heavily skewed: personal profiles far outperform company pages.
Instagram0.5–1.5%Saves and shares matter more than likes for the algorithm.
Facebook0.1–0.5%Organic reach for Pages is very low; the rate reflects that.
X0.1–0.5%High volume, fast decay. A post is largely finished within hours.
Smaller accounts look better Engagement rate falls as follower count rises, almost without exception. A 10k account at 3% and a 500k account at 0.8% may have identical content quality. Compare yourself to accounts of similar size, or to your own past.

Metrics that matter more than engagement rate

Engagement rate is a decent health check and a poor goal. If you are optimising a single number, these are better ones.

  1. Saves and shares specifically. A share puts your content in someone else's feed — it is the only engagement that directly buys distribution. A like does almost nothing by comparison. Track these separately rather than burying them in a blended rate.
  2. Follower-to-reach ratio. What share of your audience you actually reach. When this falls, distribution is shrinking regardless of how engagement looks.
  3. Profile visits and follows per post. The posts that grow an account are often not the ones with the best engagement rate.
  4. Dwell time, where the platform exposes it. On LinkedIn especially, time spent reading is now a stronger ranking signal than likes.
  5. Whatever converts. Clicks, signups, replies. Engagement is a proxy; this is the thing itself.

A reporting setup that survives contact with reality

  1. Pick one formula. Reach-based if you have reach data, follower-based if you do not.
  2. Write down what counts as an engagement, saves included or excluded, and keep it fixed.
  3. Report the median, not the mean. One post that went unusually wide will drag an average and make a normal month look like a great one.
  4. Segment by content pillar and format. A blended account-level number tells you nothing actionable. “Our teardown posts do 3x our announcement posts” does.
  5. Compare to your own trailing 90 days before comparing to anyone else's benchmark.

The practical constraint is that per-platform native analytics all define this differently, so pulling a consistent number across nine networks by hand is tedious and error-prone. Social0's analytics reports views, likes, comments, and engagement for the posts you published through it, across every connected account — with the same definition applied everywhere, which is the part that makes the trend line trustworthy.

One consistent engagement number across every network you publish to. See cross-platform analytics

The honest summary

Engagement rate is useful for spotting when something changed, and nearly useless as a target. It is easy to raise by posting less and only posting safe things, which is the opposite of what grows an account.

Use it as a smoke alarm. Optimise for shares, saves, and whatever you actually needed social media to do for the business.

Frequently asked questions

How do you calculate engagement rate on social media?

The most common formula is engagements divided by reach, times 100. You can also divide by followers (the only version comparable across accounts you do not own) or by impressions (which reads lower because it counts repeat views). Pick one and use it consistently.

What is a good engagement rate in 2026?

Roughly 3–5% on TikTok, 2–6% on LinkedIn, 0.5–1.5% on Instagram, and 0.1–0.5% on Facebook and X, measured against followers. Rates fall as follower count rises, so compare against accounts of similar size or against your own history rather than a global average.

Should saves count as engagement?

Yes, and on Instagram they are arguably the most important action — a save signals lasting value and weighs heavily in recommendations. The key is deciding once whether they are included and keeping that definition fixed, since it materially changes the number.

Why do different tools report different engagement rates?

Because they use different denominators (reach, followers, or impressions) and different definitions of what counts as an engagement. The same post can legitimately read as 1.2% in one tool and 6.5% in another. Comparing across tools is usually meaningless.

What should I track instead of engagement rate?

Shares and saves specifically, since shares are the only engagement that directly buys distribution; your follower-to-reach ratio, which reveals shrinking distribution; and whatever actually converts for you. Engagement rate works as a health check, not a goal.
